Critical

New wp2shell WordPress Core Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 7 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Updated July 18, 2026: the two flaws now carry CVE IDs, the full mechanism has been published, a persistent-object-cache condition has surfaced, and a working proof-of-concept is public. The story below reflects all of it. An anonymous HTTP request can run code on a WordPress site. The bug is in core, so a bare install with zero plugins is exploitable. Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] WordPress web server process spawns a shell/interpreter (wp2shell code execution) · [LLM] PHP webshell dropped in WordPress web root by web-server process
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse-shell egress from web-spawned interpreter on WordPress host

Anonymous request to WordPress REST batch endpoint (/batch/v1 path + query-string variant) AIDelivery High
Hunts anonymous HTTP requests to the WordPress core REST batch endpoint via BOTH exposure paths: the pretty-permalink /wp-json/batch/v1 and the query-string route rest_route=/batch/v1. Searchlight is explicit that a WAF rule covering only the /wp-json path leaves the query-string route open, so both must be watched. This is the single pre-auth exploitation primitive for wp2shell (CVE-2026-63030). Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable endpoint /wp-json/batch/v1 and its documented query-string bypass rest_route=/batch/v1 (both named by Searchlight), plus the author__not_in WP_Query SQLi parameter (CVE-2026-60137) confirmed by the WordPress GHSA advisory and Rapid7 as the injection sink — when the ?rest_route= form is used, author__not_in lands in the logged query string. No CVE scanner flags this yet, so behavioural URL-path hunting on web/WAF logs is the primary signal. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-ff9f-jf42-662q • https://blog.cloudflare.com/wordpress-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress plugins/themes (e.g. block editor, WooCommerce) that batch REST calls through /wp-json/batch/v1 for authenticated admin sessions
  • Headless/decoupled WordPress front-ends that legitimately drive the batch route from a known backend IP
  • Uptime/security scanners (wp2shell.com checker, Wordfence, Patchstack) probing the endpoint benignly
  • Internal QA or staging automation exercising REST batch calls
  • Load balancers/CDNs replaying the same URI so a single request appears from multiple source IPs
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("WordPress/","wp-cli"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all rows for the offending SrcIpAddr — check HTTP method, whether an auth cookie/nonce was present, response status, and whether the same IP hit the endpoint repeatedly with varying bodies (SQLi fuzzing). Confirm the target host's WordPress version is 6.9.0-6.9.4 or 7.0.0-7.0.1. 2) Contain: block the source IP at WAF/edge and apply a rule rejecting anonymous requests to BOTH /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1; force-update the site to 6.9.5/7.0.2. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to UC 'Web server process spawns shell interpreter' and 'PHP webshell file creation' within the minutes after the request to confirm code execution.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "/wp-json/batch/v1" or Url has "rest_route=/batch/v1" or Url has "rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1" or Url has "author__not_in"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DstIpAddr
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: WordPress REST Batch Endpoint Access (wp2shell CVE-2026-63030)
id: 6f3a1c2e-8b47-4d19-9f0a-2c7e5a1b93d4
description: Detects requests to the WordPress core REST batch endpoint via both the /wp-json path and the rest_route query-string variant (plus the author__not_in SQLi sink from CVE-2026-60137), the exploitation primitive for the wp2shell pre-auth RCE.
references:
  - https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/
  - https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-ff9f-jf42-662q
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/18
tags:
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/wp-json/batch/v1'
  selection_query:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'rest_route=/batch/v1'
      - 'rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1'
      - 'author__not_in'
  condition: selection_path or selection_query
level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/wp-json/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_path="*/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*" OR Web.uri_query="*author__not_in*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.url, Web.uri_query, Web.status, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/wp-json/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_path="*/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*" OR Web.uri_query="*author__not_in*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.url, Web.uri_query, Web.status, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
Successful (2xx) response to WordPress /batch/v1 from a first-seen source IP AIExploitation Medium
Baseline-anomaly detection: a source IP that has never previously hit the WordPress batch route now receives a successful 200/207 response on it. For a bug WordPress patched via forced updates and for which no public signature exists, a first-time source achieving success on the batch endpoint is a strong post-exploitation indicator distinct from raw request volume. Rationale: Combines the article's exact endpoint (/batch/v1) with a success-status + first-seen-source baseline — the batch route answers 207 Multi-Status on success, so an anonymous source getting 200/207 is high-signal. Baseline anti-join strips the legitimate integrations that already use the route. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://hadrian.io/blog/wp2shell-a-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-cores-rest-batch-api • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New legitimate integration or plugin deployed within the last 14 days now calling the batch route
  • A NAT/proxy rotation presenting a previously-unseen egress IP for existing authenticated admins
  • Newly onboarded monitoring/security vendor scanning the endpoint
  • CDN cache-miss origin pulls arriving from a new edge IP
  • Site migration where a new front-end host starts driving REST batch calls
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the first-seen SrcIpAddr, confirm no auth cookie/nonce accompanied the 200/207 and inspect the request body for author__not_in / UNION / stacked-query SQLi tokens. Verify the host runs a vulnerable version. 2) Contain: block the IP, force-update to 6.9.5/7.0.2, and reset DB credentials in wp-config.php if SQLi confirmed. 3) Hunt: correlate the source IP across all sites in the estate and check the affected host for shell spawns, new .php files under wp-content/uploads, and wp-config.php reads in the same window.
let lookback = 14d;
let recent = 1d;
let baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
    | where Url has "/batch/v1"
    | summarize by SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where Url has "/batch/v1"
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","207") or toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200,207)   // batch route returns 207 multi-status on success
| join kind=leftanti baseline on SrcIpAddr
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*") (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=207) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.status, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*") (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=207) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.status, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
WordPress web server process spawns a shell/interpreter (wp2shell code execution) AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation moment of wp2shell: the web tier (apache2/httpd/nginx/php-fpm/php or w3wp.exe) spawning an OS shell or scripting interpreter. On a default WordPress install these processes should never fork bash/sh/python/perl, so a web-worker-to-shell parent/child edge is a high-fidelity RCE signal. Rationale: Web-tier parent (apache2/php-fpm/w3wp) forking a shell is the textbook manifestation of the article's 'run code on a WordPress site' outcome; default WordPress never does this, giving a near-zero FP baseline. Parent+child pairing (not bare shell) keeps it alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://hadrian.io/blog/wp2shell-a-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-cores-rest-batch-api
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress plugins that legitimately shell out (e.g. some backup/image-optimisation plugins invoking convert/gzip via exec)
  • wp-cron or WP-CLI jobs run under the web user calling shell utilities
  • Server-management panels (Plesk/cPanel) driving php-fpm to run maintenance scripts
  • Composer/npm build steps executed as the web user during deploys
  • Antivirus or monitoring agents that fork helper shells under the web service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cron.php","wp-cli.phar"," wp ") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "wp-cron.php")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — reverse-shell one-liners (bash -i, python -c 'socket', nc -e), whoami/id recon, or curl-to-pipe-to-sh indicate live compromise. Note the initiating user (www-data). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and preserve the parent php-fpm worker and any dropped files for forensics; rotate DB and any secrets in wp-config.php. 3) Hunt: pivot to file writes under wp-content/uploads (webshells), outbound connections from the shell, and the preceding /batch/v1 request that seeded execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","w3wp")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","python","perl","ruby","/nc","ncat","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

PHP webshell dropped in WordPress web root by web-server process AIInstallation High
Detects a web-server/PHP process writing a .php/.phtml/.php5 file into wp-content/uploads, wp-content/plugins, or /tmp — persistence typical of WordPress RCE where the attacker drops a webshell for durable access. The uploads directory legitimately never receives executable PHP, making a web-worker-authored PHP write in that path high-fidelity. Rationale: wp-content/uploads is a static-media directory that legitimately never receives executable PHP; a web-worker-authored .php write there is a canonical webshell drop, directly following the article's RCE outcome. Path + extension + web-process author gives an alerting-grade combination. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate plugin/theme installs or auto-updates writing PHP into wp-content/plugins (usually authored by an admin session, not the raw web worker)
  • Caching plugins (WP Super Cache, W3 Total Cache) writing advanced-cache.php or config PHP into wp-content
  • Backup/migration plugins staging PHP under uploads or /tmp during restore
  • Page-builder plugins caching compiled PHP templates
  • Composer autoloader regeneration during a deploy run as the web user
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/wp-content/plugins/" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli"," wp plugin ","update-core"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file's first bytes — eval/base64_decode/assert/system/preg_replace-e or $_POST/$_GET handlers confirm a webshell. Note filename entropy and whether it sits in uploads (never legitimate). 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, block web access to the path, and audit for additional drops by the same process/hash. 3) Hunt: search all WordPress hosts for the same filename/hash, correlate to the preceding /batch/v1 request and any shell spawn, and review web logs for GET/POST to the dropped file (attacker interacting with the shell).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/uploads/","/wp-content/plugins/","\\wp-content\\uploads\\","\\wp-content\\plugins\\","/tmp/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","w3wp.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","php5","php7")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/wp-content/uploads/","/wp-content/plugins/","/tmp/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","w3wp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Hash
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

wp-config.php read/exfiltrated by shell utility on WordPress host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects an OS shell or file utility (cat/grep/curl/base64/tar/etc.) reading WordPress's wp-config.php — the file holding DB credentials and auth salts. Normal WordPress bootstrap reads this file via the PHP engine, never via cat/curl invoked from a web-worker lineage, so a shell touching wp-config.php after an RCE indicates credential theft (T1005). Rationale: wp-config.php is the credential store; article notes the SQLi->RCE chain, and exfil of DB creds/salts is the natural next step. Keying on the exact filename plus a shell utility (not the PHP engine's normal bootstrap read) isolates the theft behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/
ATT&CKT1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin or DevOps engineer legitimately grepping wp-config.php for DB settings during troubleshooting (interactive session, not web-user lineage)
  • Backup/migration tooling reading wp-config.php as part of a full-site archive
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Puppet) tasks templating or reading wp-config.php
  • Monitoring scripts that parse DB_NAME/DB_HOST from wp-config for health checks
  • Deployment pipeline copying wp-config.php between environments
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("root") and IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession == false and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("sshd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the invoking user and parent — a www-data/php-fpm parent reading wp-config.php is malicious; an interactive admin shell may be benign. Check whether output was piped to curl/nc/base64 (exfil). 2) Contain: rotate all secrets in wp-config.php (DB creds, AUTH/SECURE_AUTH/LOGGED_IN/NONCE keys and salts), rotate DB user password, and invalidate existing sessions. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections from the same host/process for the destination the file was sent to, and check the DB for injected admin users or altered options rows.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "wp-config.php"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","less","more","head","tail","curl","wget","base64","xxd","tar","cp","strings","awk","sed","nl","php")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","sh","bash","dash")
   or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","daemon")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "wp-config.php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/cat","/grep","/less","/more","/head","/tail","/curl","/wget","/base64","/xxd","/tar","/cp","/strings","/awk","/sed","/nl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: wp-config.php Read by Shell Utility (wp2shell Credential Access)
id: 1a9f6c30-2d84-4b57-9e21-6f0a3c8b74e5
description: OS shell or file utility reading WordPress wp-config.php, indicating theft of DB credentials/salts after wp2shell RCE.

Reverse-shell egress from web-spawned interpreter on WordPress host AICommand & Control Medium
Detects an OS shell/interpreter that was spawned by a WordPress web-server parent making an outbound connection to a public IP — the network callback of a reverse shell established via wp2shell. Ties the process lineage (web parent -> shell child) to the network event, distinguishing attacker C2 from a web server's normal inbound-only role. Rationale: A shell/interpreter with a web-server parent (apache2/php-fpm) beaconing to a public IP is the reverse-shell payoff of the article's RCE. Requiring the web-parent lineage keeps it out of routine sysadmin shell traffic; RemoteIPType==Public strips internal noise. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress or plugins fetching remote resources (oEmbed, Akismet, update checks) via a shell wrapper under php-fpm
  • Server monitoring/APM agents spawned from the web tier that call home over the internet
  • Composer/pip installing dependencies from public registries during a web-user deploy
  • curl/wget in a legitimate cron job under the web account pulling remote config
  • SSRF-style plugins that legitimately proxy outbound requests
Suppression filter
| where not (RemotePort in (80,443) and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("api.wordpress.org","downloads.wordpress.org","rest.akismet.com"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture RemoteIP/RemotePort and the process CommandLine — non-standard ports, raw-TCP nc/bash-tcp, or interactive-looking sessions confirm a reverse shell. Reputation-check the destination IP. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress firewall, isolate the host, and kill the process tree; the web tier should not initiate arbitrary outbound. 3) Hunt: correlate to the parent php-fpm worker, the seeding /batch/v1 request, and any wp-config.php read; sweep the estate for the same destination IP across other WordPress hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl

Unauthenticated RCE in WordPress core (wp2shell), via SQL injection

Aikido
2026-07-17 5 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

WordPress core has an unauthenticated RCE (wp2shell), confirmed as SQL injection. Update to 7.0.2 or 6.9.5 now, with mitigations if you can't patch yet. Block the attack class at runtime with Aikido Zen. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WordPress wp2shell REST batch endpoint exploitation (/wp-json/batch/v1 + author__not_in SQLi) · [LLM] Web server daemon spawning shell/interpreter after WordPress RCE (php-fpm/apache/nginx child) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Web shell PHP file written into WordPress directories by web daemon (wp2shell persistence)

WordPress wp2shell REST batch endpoint exploitation (/wp-json/batch/v1 + author__not_in SQLi) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the WordPress REST batch route that CVE-2026-63030/CVE-2026-60137 abuse, including the author__not_in WP_Query SQLi sink. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact entry-point path, the rest_route alias, and the vulnerable query parameter named in vendor corroboration. Rationale: Anchored on the exact code-block strings from the article (/wp-json/batch/v1, rest_route=/batch/v1) plus the author__not_in WP_Query sink confirmed by The Hacker News, Beazley Labs and the public PoC repo — these are high-fidelity because legitimate traffic rarely hits the batch route with these parameters. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html • https://labs.beazley.security/advisories/BSL-A1193 • https://github.com/Senanfurkan/wordpress-cve-2026-63030
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate plugins/apps that batch REST calls via /wp-json/batch/v1 (e.g. block editor bulk operations, WooCommerce sync)
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing the batch route
  • The Searchlight Cyber wp2shell.com exposure checker or blue-team validation runs
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors that exercise REST endpoints
  • Author-archive pagination legitimately passing author filters
Suppression filter
| search NOT src IN ("10.0.0.0/8","192.168.0.0/16") AND user_agent!="*Nessus*" AND user_agent!="*Qualys*" AND user_agent!="*nuclei*"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request line — confirm the source IP is external/unauthenticated and whether scStatus/ScStatus was 200 (query executed) vs 4xx (blocked/patched). Check the target host's WordPress version against 6.9.5/7.0.2/6.8.6. 2) Contain: if the host is on a vulnerable version and returned 200, block the source IP at the WAF, apply the batch-route auth mu-plugin or path block, and force the core update. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (web-daemon child processes) and UC3 (new .php files under wp-content/wp-admin) on the same host in the hours after the request to confirm code execution or web-shell drop.

| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=cIP, Method=csMethod, UriStem=csUriStem, UriQuery=csUriQuery, Status=scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent),
(AppServiceHTTPLogs

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web server daemon spawning shell/interpreter after WordPress RCE (php-fpm/apache/nginx child) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts POSIX shells, network tools and script interpreters spawned by WordPress web-server processes, the expected post-exploitation footprint of the wp2shell RCE (CVE-2026-63030). Article-specific because the flaw yields unauthenticated code execution in the PHP/web context of a WordPress host. Rationale: WordPress RCE executes in the PHP/web-server context, so a web daemon (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning a shell or download tool is the canonical execution signal; scoped to those specific parents to keep fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/wp2shell-rce-vulnerability/ • https://labs.beazley.security/advisories/BSL-A1193
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress cron/wp-cli jobs shelling out for scheduled tasks or backups
  • Plugins that legitimately call curl/wget for update checks or image processing (ImageMagick, ffmpeg wrappers)
  • Deployment/CI agents running as the web user during releases
  • Server monitoring agents invoking sh/bash health checks
  • Composer or plugin auto-updates invoking php from the web root
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cron","wp-cli","/usr/local/bin/wp") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "wp-cron.php")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp, bash -i, nc -e, pty.spawn) and the parent's command line; confirm whether the host was hit by a UC1 batch-route request minutes earlier. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate WordPress DB and secret keys (wp-config.php) since RCE ran in the web context. 3) Hunt: sweep for new/modified .php files (UC3), outbound connections from the web user, new cron entries, and modified wp-config.php across all WordPress hosts sharing the version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web shell PHP file written into WordPress directories by web daemon (wp2shell persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts creation of .php/.phtml/.phar files under WordPress content directories by a web-server or shell process, the classic web-shell persistence following the wp2shell unauthenticated RCE. Article-specific because it targets WordPress path structure (wp-content/wp-admin/wp-includes) written by the exploited web context. Rationale: Web-shell drop is the standard persistence step after a WordPress RCE; requiring the writer to be a web daemon/shell (not the package manager) and the target to be a PHP file inside WordPress content dirs keeps it aligned to the article's attack rather than routine plugin installs. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.beazley.security/advisories/BSL-A1193 • https://github.com/Senanfurkan/wordpress-cve-2026-63030
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress core/plugin/theme auto-updates writing PHP files (the article notes forced auto-updates are ON for this release)
  • wp-cli or Composer installing/updating plugins
  • Legitimate caching plugins (WP Super Cache/W3TC) generating advanced-cache.php or object-cache.php
  • CI/CD deploys pushing code to the web root
  • Developers editing theme/plugin files via the WP admin file editor
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","wp plugin","wp theme","composer","apt","dpkg","yum") or FolderPath has_any ("object-cache.php","advanced-cache.php","wp-cache-config.php"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the newly written file — look for base64/eval/gzinflate/assert/system/passthru/preg_replace-e or short obfuscated one-liners; check whether the writing process was a web daemon vs a legitimate updater (wp-cli, apt, composer). 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the file, isolate the host if the file is a confirmed web shell, and block external access to the path; rotate WordPress secrets and DB credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recently modified PHP files across wp-content/uploads (which should never contain PHP), review web access logs for GET/POST to the new filename, and check for the UC1 batch-route request and UC2 web-daemon shells preceding the write.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/","/wp-includes/","/wp-admin/")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".phar"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php","sh","bash","dash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName

OpenSSL HollowByte Flaw Could Freeze Server Memory with 11-Byte TLS Requests

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 3 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

Eleven bytes will make an unpatched OpenSSL server set aside up to 131 KB of memory for a message that never arrives. On the glibc systems Okta tested, that memory is gone until the process restarts. OpenSSL shipped the HollowByte fix in June with no CVE, no advisory, and no changelog entry pointing at it. Okta's Red Team, which reported the denial-of-service bug and named it, published the

Unpatched OpenSSL exposed to HollowByte DoS (pre-2026-06-09 build, no CVE to scan) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces OpenSSL installs on branches 3.0/3.4/3.5/3.6/4.0 below the 2026-06-09 fixed releases (3.0.21, 3.4.6, 3.5.7, 3.6.3, 4.0.1) that carry the un-numbered HollowByte TLS length-over-allocation DoS. Because HollowByte shipped with NO CVE/advisory, normal scanners miss it; this hunt keys on the raw version and on CVE-2026-34183 (the QUIC PATH_CHALLENGE DoS that shipped in the SAME June 9 train) as a proxy for a build that predates the fix. Rationale: Uses the exact fixed-release list from the article (3.0.21/3.4.6/3.5.7/3.6.3/4.0.1, dated 2026-06-09) and CVE-2026-34183 as a same-train proxy for a pre-fix build. Corroborated that CVE-2026-34183 shipped 2026-06-09 and affects 3.0/3.4/3.5/3.6/4.0 (not 1.1.1/1.0.2) via Red Hat Bugzilla and openssl-library.org, so 1.x is deliberately excluded to avoid FPs on branches whose HollowByte status is unconfirmed. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.okta.com/articles/2026/06/openssl-hollowbtye-a-dos-hiding-in-11-bytes/ • https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2481885 • https://openssl-library.org/news/vulnerabilities/ • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/06/09/15
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro-backported package (Red Hat/Debian) that reports the old base version string but already contains the patch — the article explicitly warns version reporting lies after a backport
  • OpenSSL statically linked into an appliance/container image where TVM reads the wrapper version, not the linked libssl
  • Build patched for CVE-2026-34183 but where the maintainer took the QUIC fix only and not the HollowByte TLS commit (rare, but the reason the Defender version-hunt exists alongside the CVE proxy)
  • Development / test hosts intentionally pinned to an old OpenSSL for compatibility testing
  • 4.0.1 hosts still exposed via the un-fixed DTLS path — these will NOT appear in this hunt because the TLS branch is patched
Suppression filter
| where EndOfSupportStatus != "EOS" or isempty(EndOfSupportStatus)  // optional: focus on supported builds where a backport is plausible
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm whether the host actually terminates TLS/DTLS on an internet-facing port (nginx/haproxy/httpd/stunnel) — an unlinked or loopback-only OpenSSL is low priority; check the package changelog or ask the maintainer whether they rebased on the 2026-06-09 release or cherry-picked PR 30792/30793/30794. 2) Contain: for internet-facing terminators, upgrade to the listed fixed release and restart the service (buffer only frees on process restart); if immediate patch is impossible, front the service with a proxy that fully buffers/validates the ClientHello before backend hand-off. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'OpenSSL TLS server OOM/memory-pressure' on the same hosts to see whether exploitation is already underway, and enumerate sibling hosts sharing the same golden image or package pin.
// Direct build-version hunt — catches HollowByte-vulnerable OpenSSL even where the CVE-2026-34183 proxy is patched but the un-numbered fix was not backported.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareVendor has "openssl" or SoftwareName has "openssl"
| extend Parts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1]), Patch = toint(Parts[2])
| where (Major == 3 and Minor == 0 and Patch < 21)   // 3.0.x fixed at 3.0.21
     or (Major == 3 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 6)    // 3.4.x fixed at 3.4.6
     or (Major == 3 and Minor == 5 and Patch < 7)    // 3.5.x fixed at 3.5.7
     or (Major == 3 and Minor == 6 and Patch < 3)    // 3.6.x fixed at 3.6.3
     or (Major == 4 and Minor == 0 and Patch < 1)    // 4.0.x fixed at 4.0.1
     or (Major == 3 and Minor in (1, 2, 3))          // EOL 3.x branches, no HollowByte fix shipped
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, EndOfSupportStatus
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc
// Proxy hunt: TVM still flags this OpenSSL for CVE-2026-34183 (shipped in the same 2026-06-09 release as the un-numbered HollowByte fix) => build predates the fix => also HollowByte-vulnerable.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "openssl"
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-34183"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc

OpenSSL TLS server OOM-kill / memory pressure (HollowByte glibc heap fragmentation) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the HollowByte impact signature: an OpenSSL-linked TLS-terminating server (nginx, httpd/apache2, haproxy, stunnel) killed by the Linux OOM-killer or emitting OOM/oom_reaper events. HollowByte's distinguishing trait is that freed buffers never return to the kernel on glibc, so RSS climbs and stays climbed until the process is OOM-killed — without ever crossing a connection ceiling. Rationale: Keys on the article's/Okta's stated impact: glibc keeps freed small/medium chunks so RSS 'stays climbed long after the attacker has gone' and the server is 'OOM-killed' (nginx named explicitly). The kernel OOM-killer line ('Out of memory: Killed process N (nginx)') plus a TLS-terminator process name is high-fidelity and article-specific. Defender AH has no OOM ActionType for Linux, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; the signal lives in kernel syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.okta.com/articles/2026/06/openssl-hollowbtye-a-dos-hiding-in-11-bytes/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hollowbyte-ddos-flaw-bloats-openssl-server-memory-with-11-byte-payload/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1499.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuinely undersized VM where nginx/haproxy is OOM-killed under legitimate peak traffic, not attack
  • A memory leak in a web-app module (PHP-FPM, mod_php) rather than in OpenSSL's handshake buffers
  • cgroup/container memory-limit kills (memory.max) on a co-located sidecar that names the TLS process incidentally
  • Batch/cron jobs on the same host spiking memory and triggering global OOM that reaps the web server as the largest RSS consumer
  • Kubernetes eviction storms that surface as OOM messages referencing the ingress-nginx pod
Suppression filter
| where SampleMessage !has "memory.max" and SampleMessage !has "cgroup"  // drop container memory-limit kills; keep global/host OOM which matches the HollowByte host-exhaustion pattern
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the OOM victim is an internet-facing TLS terminator and correlate the kill timestamps with a rising RSS trend on that PID (node_exporter/process metrics) and with source-IP diversity of half-open/never-completed TLS connections at the LB — HollowByte holds workers on bodies that never arrive. 2) Contain: restart the affected service to reclaim the frozen glibc arenas (memory only returns on process restart), then patch OpenSSL to the 2026-06-09 fixed release (3.0.21/3.4.6/3.5.7/3.6.3/4.0.1) and, as a stopgap, set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX / front with a fully-buffering proxy and lower handshake timeouts. 3) Hunt: run UC 'Unpatched OpenSSL exposed to HollowByte' across the fleet to find every host on a pre-fix build, and review perimeter logs for sources opening many TLS connections that send only a tiny ClientHello then go silent.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Facility in ("kern", "syslog", "daemon")
| where SyslogMessage has "Out of memory" or SyslogMessage has "oom-kill" or SyslogMessage has "oom_reaper"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("nginx", "openssl", "httpd", "apache2", "haproxy", "stunnel")
| summarize KillCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostName, Facility
| where KillCount >= 2   // 2 = repeated OOM of a TLS terminator within the window; single OOMs are common one-offs
| sort by KillCount desc

Installation of ViteVenom malicious scoped npm packages (@vitejs typosquats) AIDelivery High
Hunts installation or lockfile presence of the seven named ViteVenom packages that impersonate the @vitejs/* namespace to deliver the ChainVeil blockchain-loaded RAT. Article-specific because it keys on the exact scoped package identifiers published Jun 29–Jul 3 2026, not a generic npm-install pattern. Rationale: Uses the seven exact scoped package names Checkmarx published for ViteVenom (@uw010010/vite-tree, @vite-tab/tab, @vite-ln/build-ts, @vite-mcp/vite-type, @vite-pro/vite-ui, @vitets/vite-ts, @vite-ts/vite-ui) — literal IOCs, so any hit is high-fidelity regardless of blockchain-stage behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/supply-chain-attack-smart/ • https://news.backbox.org/2026/07/17/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use-blockchain-c2-to-deliver-a-rat/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally reproducing the IOC in an isolated malware-analysis sandbox
  • Security tooling / dependency scanners echoing the package names in their own command lines
  • Internal threat-intel scripts grepping build hosts for these names
  • A private package that coincidentally shares one of these names in a monorepo path string
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm audit" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "grep" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\SecurityTools\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the package name is one of the seven and pull package-lock.json / yarn.lock to see if it resolved from the public registry vs an internal mirror; check registration/install timestamp against Jun 29–Jul 3 2026. 2) Contain: isolate the dev/build host, delete node_modules and the lockfile entry, and force-rotate every credential the developer/CI had (tokens, SSH keys, cloud keys) since the RAT harvests credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (blockchain C2 egress from node) and UC3 (shell-profile persistence) on the same host, and search other repos/CI runners for the same package strings.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","node","yarn.exe","yarn","pnpm.exe","pnpm") or FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@uw010010/vite-tree","@vite-tab/tab","@vite-ln/build-ts","@vite-mcp/vite-type","@vite-pro/vite-ui","@vitets/vite-ts","@vite-ts/vite-ui")

| order by Timestamp desc

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@uw010010/vite-tree","@vite-tab/tab","@vite-ln/build-ts","@vite-mcp/vite-type","@vite-pro/vite-ui","@vitets/vite-ts","@vite-ts/vite-ui")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node/Vite build process contacting Tron, Aptos or BSC blockchain C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the ChainVeil loader resolving its next-stage payload pointer from public blockchains — a node/vite/esbuild process reaching Tron (TronGrid/Tronscan), Aptos (aptoslabs) or Binance Smart Chain (BSCScan/bsc-dataseed) endpoints. Blockchain RPC/explorer traffic originating from a build toolchain is the campaign's defining, near-untakedownable C2 behaviour. Rationale: Article states the loader queries Tron for the latest attacker-wallet tx, falls back to Aptos, and pivots to a BSC transaction — so egress from node/vite to these three chains' public RPC/explorer hosts is the campaign's signature; scoping to a build-toolchain parent process removes generic dApp browsing noise. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/supply-chain-attack-smart/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/dApp developers whose node build genuinely queries TronGrid/BSCScan/Aptos APIs
  • Blockchain analytics or wallet-tooling packages that call these endpoints as a feature
  • CI pipelines for crypto projects running contract verification against BSCScan
  • A developer's local script polling Aptos/Tron balances during testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("hardhat","truffle","web3","ethers","@aptos-labs","tronweb")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating node/vite process and its working directory — is this a web3/crypto repo (likely benign) or a generic frontend build (highly suspicious)? Capture the full RemoteUrl and any subsequent HTTP fallback to a raw C2. 2) Contain: block the resolved IPs at egress for non-crypto build hosts and isolate the host; the blockchain pointer is immutable so focus on cutting the host's outbound path. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (were any of the seven packages installed?) and check for a direct HTTP fallback fetch of the RAT bypassing the blockchain, plus UC3 persistence and UC4 shell spawns.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","vite.exe","vite","esbuild.exe","esbuild")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("trongrid.io","tronscanapi.com","tronscan.org","aptoslabs.com","aptoscan.com","bscscan.com","bsc-dataseed","binance.org")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Endpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("trongrid.io","tronscanapi.com","tronscan.org","aptoslabs.com","aptoscan.com","bscscan.com","bsc-dataseed","binance.org")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Domains=make_set(DnsQuery,10) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

Unix shell profile (.bashrc/.zshrc/.profile) modified by npm/node build process AIInstallation High
Hunts the ViteVenom RAT establishing persistent backdoor injection by writing to shell startup files — the exact artefacts Checkmarx tells victims to audit. Article-specific because it ties a .bashrc/.zshrc/.profile change to a node/npm/vite parent rather than flagging all profile edits. Rationale: Article explicitly directs victims to 'look for unauthorized modifications to .bashrc, .zshrc, and .profile files'; constraining the writer to a node/npm/vite toolchain parent turns that guidance into a low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://news.backbox.org/2026/07/17/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use-blockchain-c2-to-deliver-a-rat/
ATT&CKT1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • nvm / fnm / volta install scripts appending PATH lines to .bashrc/.zshrc
  • oh-my-zsh or Starship prompt installers editing .zshrc
  • A postinstall that legitimately adds a CLI completion hook to the shell rc
  • Developer manually editing their own rc via an editor spawned from a terminal (parent would not be node — filtered)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("nvm","fnm","volta","oh-my-zsh","starship","rustup","pyenv")
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the shell profile against version control/backup and inspect the appended line — a base64 blob, curl|bash, or reverse-shell one-liner confirms malicious injection vs a benign PATH edit. 2) Contain: remove the injected line, isolate the host, kill any RAT process spawned from the rc, and rotate the developer's credentials. 3) Hunt: check every interactive shell session since the write for spawned reverse shells (UC4), and sweep other dev hosts for the same rc line and the UC1 packages.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ (".bashrc",".zshrc",".profile",".bash_profile",".zprofile")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","vite","esbuild","sh","bash","zsh") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","npm","vite")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".zshrc",".profile",".bash_profile",".zprofile")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","vite","esbuild","sh","bash","zsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node/Vite build process spawning shell with reverse-shell indicators (import-time RAT execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the import-time execution stage where the ChainVeil RAT launches a reverse shell — a node/vite/esbuild parent spawning bash/sh/cmd/powershell with reverse-shell or download markers. Targets execution behaviour the campaign hides by running at import rather than install time. Rationale: Article says the RAT provides a reverse shell and that code runs at import time via the build toolchain, so a node/vite parent spawning a shell with /dev/tcp, bash -i, nc -e or encoded-PS markers captures execution while the reverse-shell markers strip legitimate build-script shell-outs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/supply-chain-attack-smart/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / prebuild native module builds legitimately spawning sh and invoking curl/wget for binaries
  • A build script that shells out to curl to fetch assets during CI
  • postinstall lifecycle scripts running bash helpers (parent node)
  • Developer running a make/compile step that pipes through sh with -i in an interactive tool
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","node-pre-gyp","cmake-js") and ProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and the network destination of any curl/wget or /dev/tcp target; a non-package, non-registry IP or a raw C2 host confirms malicious egress. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and block the reverse-shell destination; preserve the node parent command line for the offending package path. 3) Hunt: map the node parent back to the installed package (UC1), check for blockchain C2 resolution just prior (UC2) and shell-profile persistence just after (UC3), and rotate all credentials reachable from the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","vite","esbuild")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","curl","wget")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","bash -i","sh -i","nc -e","-e /bin","-EncodedCommand","Invoke-Expression","IEX(","curl ","wget ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","vite","esbuild")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","curl","wget")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","bash -i","sh -i","nc -e","-e /bin","-EncodedCommand","Invoke-Expression","IEX(","curl ","wget ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)

| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

New NadMesh Botnet Hunts Exposed AI Services for Cloud Keys and Kubernetes Tokens

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 14 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Go botnet called NadMesh turned up in early July hunting exposed AI services, and the operator's own dashboard claims 3,811 unique AWS keys. A Shodan harvester keeps the scan queue stocked with ComfyUI, Ollama, n8n, Open WebUI, Langflow, and Gradio: the image generators, local model runners, and workflow builders that teams stand up fast and firewall late. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internal host mass-scanning AI service ports 8188/11434/7860/5678 (NadMesh Shodan-style sweep) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Exposed Docker Engine API on 2375 hit from the internet (NadMesh top vector)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposed AI/DevOps service exploited: pre-auth RCE endpoints hit + service spawns shell to fetch NadMesh
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] NadMesh Linux persistence: hidden drop files in /dev/shm, /tmp and stealth cron.d entries · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New NadMesh Botnet Hunts Exposed AI Services for Cloud Keys and Kubernetes Token
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NadMesh C2 callback to 209.99.186.235 / cdnorigin.net or agent SHA1 execution · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NadMesh cloud-credential harvesting: reads of ~/.aws, .env, ~/.docker/config.json and cloud env vars · [LLM] Kubernetes ServiceAccount token / kubeconfig access by bot processes and anonymous secret reads · [LLM] Kubernetes privilege escalation via stolen tokens: anonymous/SA creating ClusterRoleBindings · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
NadMesh Linux persistence: hidden drop files in /dev/shm, /tmp and stealth cron.d entries AIInstallation High
Hunts NadMesh's on-disk persistence artefacts on Linux hosts: hidden agent binaries dropped as .a under /dev/shm, /var/tmp and /tmp, and dot-prefixed cron jobs /etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor and /etc/cron.d/.s. These exact paths are XLab's published NadMesh drop paths and are article-specific rather than generic Linux persistence. Rationale: Uses XLab's exact published NadMesh drop paths (/dev/shm/.a, /var/tmp/.a, /tmp/.a, /etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor, /etc/cron.d/.s) - these fixed hidden filenames are high-fidelity and not generic. Corroborated against the gbhackers write-up of the same XLab report. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/ • https://cyberpress.org/nadmesh-targets-ai-servers/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Config-management tools (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) that legitimately deploy /etc/cron.d entries - though rarely dot-prefixed
  • Backup or monitoring agents that stage files in /dev/shm
  • A sysadmin manually testing cron with a throwaway .s file
  • Container runtimes writing scratch files named .a in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the file contents and hash; confirm the .a binary is Garble/UPX-packed (high entropy, UPX header) and read the cron file's command line to find the callback URL/IP. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network; NadMesh uses triple-redundant persistence so kill all agent processes AND remove every drop file + cron entry together before the survivors respawn it. 3) Hunt: on the same host check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for unknown keys, then revoke (not rotate) every credential the host could reach - AWS keys, k8s tokens, .env, registry logins - and pivot to UC2 to find the C2 channel.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has "/etc/cron.d/" and FileName in~ (".sys_monitor",".s"))
    or (FileName == ".a" and FolderPath has_any ("/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/tmp/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (TargetFilePath has "/etc/cron.d/" and TargetFileName in~ (".sys_monitor",".s"))
    or (TargetFileName == ".a" and TargetFilePath has_any ("/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/tmp/"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NadMesh Botnet Linux Persistence Drop Files and Stealth Cron
id: 8f2c1d4a-6b3e-4a9c-9d1f-2e7a5c8b0f31
description: Detects NadMesh botnet on-disk persistence artefacts - hidden .a agent binaries under /dev/shm,/var/tmp,/tmp and dot-prefixed cron.d entries .sys_monitor/.s
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html
  - https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/18
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.003
  - attack.t1564.001
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_hidden:
    TargetFilename:
      - '/dev/shm/.a'
      - '/var/tmp/.a'
      - '/tmp/.a'
  selection_cron:
    TargetFilename:
      - '/etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor'
      - '/etc/cron.d/.s'
  condition: selection_hidden or selection_cron
falsepositives:
  - Rare legitimate admin scripts using dot-prefixed cron files
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH (@file.path:("/dev/shm/.a" OR "/var/tmp/.a" OR "/tmp/.a" OR "/etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor" OR "/etc/cron.d/.s"))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\/(dev\/shm|var\/tmp|tmp)\/\.a$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/etc\/cron\.d\/\.(sys_monitor|s)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path IN ("/dev/shm/.a","/var/tmp/.a","/tmp/.a","/etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor","/etc/cron.d/.s")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path IN ("/dev/shm/.a","/var/tmp/.a","/tmp/.a","/etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor","/etc/cron.d/.s")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
NadMesh C2 callback to 209.99.186.235 / cdnorigin.net or agent SHA1 execution AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host contacting NadMesh's published C2 infrastructure - IP 209.99.186.235 or domain cdnorigin.net - or executing the published agent sample SHA1 31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec. Pure-IOC detection tied directly to XLab's indicator list. Rationale: Directly uses XLab's three published NadMesh indicators (C2 IP 209.99.186.235, domain cdnorigin.net, agent SHA1 31c69b3e...). Because every build is Garble/UPX-repacked to a unique hash, the network IOCs are the durable anchor and the SHA1 catches only the one published build. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared-hosting/CDN reuse if 209.99.186.235 is later re-leased to benign tenants - re-verify IP is still flagged
  • Security scanners/sandboxes in your org intentionally detonating the sample and beaconing to the C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling resolving cdnorigin.net for lookups rather than a real infection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process and user; correlate the connection time with UC1 drop-file writes and UC5 exploit chain on the same host to establish infection vs. scanner. 2) Contain: block 209.99.186.235 and cdnorigin.net at the perimeter and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep all netflow/proxy for any other host that touched the same IOCs, and immediately begin credential revocation (AWS/k8s/.env/registry) for every affected host per XLab guidance - revoke before rotating.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "209.99.186.235"
    or RemoteUrl has "cdnorigin.net"
    or InitiatingProcessSHA1 == "31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA1, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "209.99.186.235" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcAction),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "cdnorigin.net" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NadMesh C2 Network Connection to Known Infrastructure

NadMesh cloud-credential harvesting: reads of ~/.aws, .env, ~/.docker/config.json and cloud env vars AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts NadMesh's credential-collection behaviour on compromised Linux hosts: shell utilities reading ~/.aws/config and credentials, .env files, ~/.docker/config.json, or scraping cloud secret environment variables (AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, KUBECONFIG). These are the exact loot targets XLab observed being shipped home. Rationale: Anchored on XLab's explicit loot list: cloud keys from env vars, contents of ~/.aws/config, .env and ~/.docker/config.json. Scoping to shell/read utilities plus these paths/varnames keeps it far tighter than a generic 'someone read a file' rule. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/ • https://cyberpress.org/nadmesh-targets-ai-servers/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD runners (GitLab/Jenkins agents) reading .env and .aws/credentials during builds
  • Developers running `aws configure` / cat-ing their own ~/.aws/config interactively
  • Container entrypoint scripts that echo or grep AWS_/KUBECONFIG env vars at startup
  • Backup jobs tar-ing home directories that include .aws and .docker
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitlab-runner","buildkitd","jenkins-agent") and ActorUsername !endswith "-ci"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process - if the reader was spawned by an exposed AI/DevOps service (python/marimo/rclone/node/dockerd) or an unexpected shell, treat as malicious; if it is a known CI runner or interactive admin session, likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host and revoke every credential the process touched (AWS keys, docker registry logins, .env secrets) - revoke, do not rotate, until persistence is removed. 3) Hunt: check for outbound POST/exfil to the C2 (UC2) shortly after the reads, and pivot to any Kubernetes token access (UC4) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine contains ".aws/" or ProcessCommandLine contains ".docker/config.json" or ProcessCommandLine contains ".env" or ProcessCommandLine contains "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" or ProcessCommandLine contains "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS")
    or (FileName in~ ("env","printenv") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AWS_","GOOGLE_","AZURE_","KUBECONFIG"))
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","head","tail","cp","tar","base64","xxd","strings","awk","less","more","curl","env","printenv","sh","bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cat","grep","head","tail","cp","tar","base64","env","printenv","curl","sh","bash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains ".aws/" or ActingProcessCommandLine contains ".docker/config.json" or ActingProcessCommandLine contains ".env" or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS" or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "KUBECONFIG"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kubernetes ServiceAccount token / kubeconfig access by bot processes and anonymous secret reads AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts NadMesh's Kubernetes credential theft: process access to the in-pod ServiceAccount token (/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token), ~/.kube/config or KUBECONFIG, plus API-server GET/LIST of secrets by anonymous or serviceaccount principals. Article states NadMesh explicitly hunts k8s service-account tokens and cluster privileges. Rationale: Uses the canonical in-pod SA token path /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token plus kubeconfig/KUBECONFIG, matching XLab's statement that NadMesh targets k8s service-account tokens and cluster privileges. The AKSAudit arm catches anonymous/SA secret enumeration that follows token theft. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • kubectl and in-cluster operators/controllers routinely reading the SA token
  • Service meshes / logging agents mounting and reading the token by design
  • Legitimate anonymous read on public health endpoints (not secrets) - excluded by resource=secrets filter
  • Backup tooling tar-ing container filesystems that include the token mount
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "kubectl/" and UserAgent !startswith "kube-controller-manager"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process reading the token is NOT a legitimate in-cluster controller by checking its image/parent - a shell (sh/bash) or curl reading the token from a service pod is malicious. 2) Contain: delete/roll the compromised ServiceAccount token, cordon the node/pod, and rotate the SA. 3) Hunt: review AKSAudit for that SA creating ClusterRoleBindings or listing secrets cluster-wide (pivot to UC8), and check for external egress of the token to the C2 (UC2).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount", "/.kube/config", "KUBECONFIG")
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","curl","wget","base64","tar","cp","head","kubectl","sh","bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("get","list","watch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "secrets"
| extend Requestor = tostring(User.username)
| where Requestor == "system:anonymous" or Requestor startswith "system:serviceaccount:"
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ResponseStatus = tostring(ResponseStatus.code)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
