Exposed AI/DevOps service exploited: pre-auth RCE endpoints hit + service spawns shell to fetch NadMesh AIExploitation Medium
Detects the NadMesh initial-access chain against exposed services: web requests to the specific pre-auth RCE endpoints it weaponises (Marimo /terminal/ws CVE-2026-39987, rclone /options/set NoAuth flip CVE-2026-41176, Jenkins /scriptText, Spring Cloud Gateway /actuator/gateway/routes CVE-2022-22947, MCP JSON-RPC execute_command), and the host-side result of an AI/DevOps service process spawning a shell that curls/wgets the payload. Rationale: Combines corroborated CVE endpoints - Marimo /terminal/ws (CVE-2026-39987, confirmed by Endor/CSA) and rclone /options/set NoAuth (CVE-2026-41176, confirmed by Endor/NVD) - plus Jenkins /scriptText, Spring /actuator/gateway/routes (CVE-2022-22947) and MCP execute_command from the article's exploit chart, with the host-side signal of these exact services spawning a shell to pull the payload into the /dev/shm or /tmp/.a drop paths. Cross-checked against: • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-41176 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41176 • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/root-in-one-request-marimos-critical-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-39987 • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-marimo-rce-cve-2026-39987-ai-toolchain-202/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of the Jenkins /scriptText console by a Jenkins admin
  • rclone RC API called by authenticated automation (options/set from an internal orchestrator)
  • A data-science service legitimately shelling out to curl a model/dataset from an internal mirror
  • Vulnerability scanners in the org probing /actuator and /terminal/ws endpoints
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0/8") or Url has_any ("/terminal/ws","/core/command")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the web arm, check the source IP reputation and whether the request succeeded (200/101); for the host arm, read the full child command line to capture the download URL and payload path. 2) Contain: put the exposed service behind auth or off the internet, isolate the host, and block the download URL/C2. 3) Hunt: confirm the fetched binary matches the NadMesh drop paths (UC1) and C2 (UC2), and check whether credential harvesting (UC3/UC4) already ran on the host before isolation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rclone","marimo","python","python3","java","node","dockerd","gunicorn","uvicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/dev/shm","/tmp/.a","/var/tmp/.a","chmod +x","base64 -d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/terminal/ws","/options/set","/config/set","/core/command","/scriptText","/actuator/gateway/routes")
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","101","201") or isempty(tostring(HttpStatusCode))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(rclone|marimo|python3?|java|node|dockerd|gunicorn|uvicorn)/i ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|curl|wget)$/i
| CommandLine=/(curl|wget|\/dev\/shm|\/tmp\/\.a|chmod \+x|base64 -d)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("rclone","marimo","python","python3","java","node","dockerd") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget") AND (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/shm*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/.a*" OR Processes.process="*chmod +x*" OR Processes.process="*base64 -d*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("rclone","marimo","python","python3","java","node","dockerd") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget") AND (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/shm*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/.a*" OR Processes.process="*chmod +x*" OR Processes.process="*base64 -d*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Exposed Docker Engine API on 2375 hit from the internet (NadMesh top vector) AIDelivery Medium
Detects inbound connections to an unauthenticated Docker Engine API on TCP 2375, the single largest slice (30.31%) of NadMesh's observed exploit traffic (docker_containers_api_rce). Flags the exposed-socket condition the article calls out explicitly. Rationale: Port 2375 is the concrete, article-named exposed Docker socket that carries the plurality (30.31%) of NadMesh's exploit traffic; inbound public connections to it are a direct, low-ambiguity signal of the exposed-service condition the article warns about. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/ • https://cyberpress.org/nadmesh-targets-ai-servers/
ATT&CKT1610 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD or orchestration that (insecurely) uses plaintext 2375 instead of TLS 2376
  • Vulnerability scanners / attack-surface-management tools probing 2375
  • Container monitoring agents polling the Docker API over TCP
  • Legacy Swarm setups still listening on 2375 internally
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr != "127.0.0.1" and not ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether 2375 is genuinely internet-reachable and whether the source IP is external; check dockerd for recently created privileged containers with host-path mounts. 2) Contain: firewall 2375 off the internet and switch the daemon to TLS-authenticated 2376; kill any attacker-spawned containers. 3) Hunt: inspect created containers for host filesystem mounts used to read ~/.aws / k8s tokens (UC3/UC4) and check for the NadMesh drop files (UC1) and C2 (UC2).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort == 2375 or RemotePort == 2375
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 2375
| where NetworkDirection == "Inbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkDirection, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internal host mass-scanning AI service ports 8188/11434/7860/5678 (NadMesh Shodan-style sweep) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a compromised host performing NadMesh's AI-service reconnaissance: one source rapidly connecting to many distinct IPs on the four ports the rescan job puts first - 8188 (ComfyUI), 11434 (Ollama), 7860 (Gradio), 5678 (n8n). Threshold correlation flags the /24 sweep behaviour the article describes. Rationale: Uses the exact four ports the article says NadMesh's rescan job puts first (8188 ComfyUI, 11434 Ollama, 7860 Gradio, 5678 n8n) and the /24-sweep behaviour; a single internal host fanning out to 50+ targets on these ports in 15m is a scanning signature, not normal client traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1046 T1595.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate central ML gateway/load-balancer fanning out to many Ollama/ComfyUI backends
  • Internal vulnerability scanners and asset-inventory tools probing these ports
  • Kubernetes service discovery hitting many pod IPs on model-serving ports
  • A CI job load-testing an inference fleet
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("litellm","traefik","nginx","envoy","kube-proxy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the scanning process and user on the source host; a non-inference binary (or a shell/Go binary in /tmp) fanning out is malicious, whereas a known gateway service is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the source host and block its outbound scanning. 3) Hunt: on the source host look for NadMesh drop files (UC1) and C2 (UC2); on any target that responded, check whether exploitation and credential theft followed (UC5/UC3/UC4).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemotePort in (8188, 11434, 7860, 5678)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), Attempts = count()
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 15m)
| where DistinctTargets > 50   // one host probing 50+ distinct IPs on AI ports in 15m = sweep, not client use
| order by DistinctTargets desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DstPortNumber in (8188, 11434, 7860, 5678)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DstIpAddr), Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber), Attempts = count()
    by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DistinctTargets > 50   // sweep threshold across the four NadMesh-prioritised AI ports
| order by DistinctTargets desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=8188 OR RemotePort=11434 OR RemotePort=7860 OR RemotePort=5678)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=distinct_targets))
| distinct_targets > 50
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action
| filter dstPort in [8188, 11434, 7860, 5678] and action = "ACCEPT"
| stats count_distinct(dstAddr) as targets, count(*) as attempts by srcAddr
| sort targets desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (8188,11434,7860,5678) by All_Traffic.src _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_targets > 50
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (8188,11434,7860,5678) by All_Traffic.src _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_targets > 50
Kubernetes privilege escalation via stolen tokens: anonymous/SA creating ClusterRoleBindings AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-compromise Kubernetes lateral movement using stolen ServiceAccount tokens: create/update of ClusterRoleBindings, ClusterRoles or RoleBindings by system:anonymous or a serviceaccount principal, especially binding to cluster-admin/admin. Covers the cluster-privilege objective the article attributes to NadMesh. Rationale: Grounded in the article's statement that NadMesh is after 'Kubernetes cluster privileges' - creation of ClusterRoleBindings/ClusterRoles by anonymous or serviceaccount principals is the concrete API-audit expression of stolen-token privilege escalation. Defender/Falcon left empty because K8s API audit is not in DeviceProcessEvents or FDR. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/ • https://cyberpress.org/nadmesh-targets-ai-servers/
ATT&CKT1098 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GitOps/CD controllers (ArgoCD/Flux) running as a serviceaccount that legitimately manage RBAC
  • Helm chart installs that create ClusterRoles/Bindings during deploy
  • Cluster bootstrap operators reconciling RBAC on startup
  • A platform team's automation SA that owns RBAC by design
Suppression filter
| where Requestor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and Requestor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:" and UserAgent !startswith "helm"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the requesting SA and its source pod/IP; compare against your known GitOps/RBAC-owning identities - an unexpected SA or system:anonymous binding to cluster-admin is malicious. 2) Contain: delete the rogue ClusterRoleBinding, revoke/rotate the SA token, and cordon the originating pod/node. 3) Hunt: trace back to which pod's token was used (correlate with UC4 token access), review AKSAudit for secrets exfiltration by the same SA, and audit all bindings created in the window.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in ("clusterrolebindings","clusterroles","rolebindings")
| extend Requestor = tostring(User.username), BoundRole = tostring(RequestObject.roleRef.name)
| where Requestor == "system:anonymous" or Requestor startswith "system:serviceaccount:"
| project TimeGenerated, Requestor, Verb, Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), ObjName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), BoundRole, UserAgent, ResponseStatus = tostring(ResponseStatus.code)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(clusterrolebindings OR clusterroles OR rolebindings) @user.username:(system:anonymous OR system:serviceaccount:*)
CLOUD
index=kubernetes (sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" OR sourcetype="aws:eks:audit") verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("clusterrolebindings","clusterroles","rolebindings") ("user.username"="system:anonymous" OR "user.username"="system:serviceaccount:*") | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(objectRef.name) as objects values(requestObject.roleRef.name) as boundRole by user.username verb objectRef.resource | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or SHA1 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or MD5 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or SHA1 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or MD5 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoldenEyeDog .scr payload extracted from ZIP delivered via support/chat channel AIDelivery High
Hunts the CylindricalCanine initial-access technique: a ZIP disguised as a customer screenshot containing a .scr executable, dropped and run from a browser/archiver/chat/support client. Article-specific because the actor delivers .scr screensaver payloads through customer-support chat rather than classic email attachments. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit initial-access artifact — a ZIP disguised as a customer screenshot containing a .scr executable delivered via customer-support chat. The .scr extension launched from Temp/Downloads by an archiver/browser/chat parent is very rare in enterprise and distinguishes this from generic email malware. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/digicert-hacked-screensaver/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1566.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy .scr screensaver files packaged in software installers and extracted by 7-Zip/WinRAR
  • Corporate screensaver policy deployment copying .scr files to user profiles
  • Developer/QA testing screensaver builds from a Downloads folder
  • Self-extracting archives that legitimately contain .scr helpers
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Windows\Web\Screen") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "screensaver-deploy")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the SHA256 of the .scr and detonate/VT-check it; review the source chat/support ticket or download referrer and the process tree for a follow-on DLL-side-load host process. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the .scr process tree, and quarantine the parent ZIP; disable the affected support-analyst account if the file arrived via a support portal. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for update.log payload drops (UC2), the C2 IPs/qaqkongtiao.com (UC4), and other analysts who received screenshot ZIPs in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".scr"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Packages\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("7zFM.exe","7z.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe","explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe","teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","slack.exe","zoom.exe")

Golden Gh0st Loader DLL side-load with encrypted update.log payload AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the CylindricalCanine execution stage: a legitimate signed EXE running from a user-writable directory side-loads a rogue DLL that then reads an encrypted payload named update.log. Correlates a user-path DLL image load with an update.log file drop on the same host within a short window. Rationale: Anchored on the article's specific side-load chain — a legitimate executable running a rogue DLL that loads an encrypted payload named 'update.log' while showing a decoy 503 PDF. The DLL-load-from-user-path + update.log co-occurrence is the malware's distinctive on-disk footprint; Elastic corroborates the same actor's encrypted-image-payload side-load pattern (tp.png in RONINGLOADER). Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/roningloader • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate portable apps run from Downloads/AppData that write an update.log alongside their DLLs
  • Auto-updaters (Squirrel/Electron apps) dropping update.log in AppData
  • Software running from ProgramData that side-loads its own plugin DLLs
  • Developer builds executing binaries from a Temp working directory
Suppression filter
| where HostExe !in~ ("update.exe","squirrel.exe","electron.exe") and HostExePath !has @"\Microsoft\Teams\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Collect the host EXE, the side-loaded DLL, and update.log; verify the EXE's signature/original filename vs. its folder, and submit the DLL + update.log for analysis. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the side-load host process, and quarantine the EXE/DLL/update.log triad. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host EXE hash and update.log path across the fleet, and correlate to the .scr delivery (UC1) and outbound C2 (UC4) from the same device.
let Window = 10m;
let PayloadDrops = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "update.log"
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Roaming\")
    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, PayloadTime = Timestamp, PayloadFolder = FolderPath, DropProc = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| join kind=inner PayloadDrops on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (PayloadTime - Window .. PayloadTime + Window)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LoadedDLL = FileName, DLLPath = FolderPath, HostExe = InitiatingProcessFileName, HostExePath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, PayloadFolder, PayloadTime
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "update.log"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Roaming\")
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\Windows\" and ActingProcessName !has @"\Program Files"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\update.log OR *\Update.log OR *\UPDATE.LOG) AND @TargetFilename:(*\AppData\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\Public\* OR *\ProgramData\*) AND NOT @Image:(*\Windows\* OR *\Program?Files*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\update\.log$/i
| regex("\\\\(AppData|Temp|Public|ProgramData|Roaming)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(Windows|Program Files)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="update.log" (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Public\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search NOT (process_name IN ("svchost.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe","MsMpEng.exe")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="update.log" (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Public\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search NOT (process_name IN ("svchost.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe","MsMpEng.exe")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Execution of known Golden Gh0st RAT / Zhong Stealer artifacts (stolen-cert-signed) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on execution, load, or drop of files whose SHA256 matches Golden Gh0st Loader / Golden Gh0st RAT / Zhong Stealer samples — including binaries the actor signed with EV code-signing certificates stolen from DigiCert. Because Defender AH exposes no Authenticode-issuer column, this pivots on corroborated file hashes rather than certificate thumbprints. Rationale: Uses the 13 SHA256 IOCs provided with the article and independently corroborated by Elastic's RONINGLOADER report (matching da2c…, c65170…, 2515b… ollama.sys, 1613a… tp.png). Directly implements the reviewer's stolen-DigiCert-cert-signed-malware detection, pivoting to hash IOCs because Defender AH has no signer/issuer column to match the revoked DigiCert G4 CAs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/roningloader • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/
ATT&CKT1553.006 T1588.003 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC detonating the sample in a sanctioned malware lab
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the hash retained on an admin host
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling caching the file for analysis
  • Hash collision is effectively impossible for SHA256 — near-zero benign hits
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARE-LAB-01","IR-SANDBOX-01")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the hit is not a sanctioned analysis host; capture the file path, signer, and parent process. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the endpoint, block the hash tenant-wide, and if the binary carries a DigiCert EV signature confirm the cert is among the 60 DigiCert-revoked certificates and submit for revocation validation. Step 3 (hunt): Expand to the side-load host EXE and update.log (UC2), C2 IPs/qaqkongtiao.com (UC4), and query DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for any other binaries signed by the same revoked cert serials.

Golden Gh0st RAT C2 to GoldenEyeDog infrastructure (IPs + qaqkongtiao.com) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on outbound connections or DNS resolutions to CylindricalCanine C2 infrastructure — seven hard IOC IPs and the domain qaqkongtiao.com used by Golden Gh0st RAT (which also opens a SOCKS proxy tunnel). Surfaces the initiating process so an analyst can pivot to the side-loaded host binary. Rationale: Uses the seven hard C2 IP IOCs and the qaqkongtiao.com domain shipped with the article and published in Expel's GoldenEyeDog IOC bundle; projecting the initiating process ties the C2 beacon back to the side-loading host binary for one-hop pivoting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/expel-io/expel-intel/blob/main/2026/07/GoldenEyeDog-IOC/Golden_Gh0st_IOCs.csv • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A VPS in one of the /24s later re-leased to a benign tenant (IP reuse)
  • Security scanner or threat-intel crawler in your org proactively probing the IOC IPs
  • Shared-hosting IP that also fronts unrelated legitimate sites
  • Sinkhole/passive-DNS research traffic to qaqkongtiao.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nmap.exe","nessus.exe","masscan.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Nessus\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and confirm it is not a browser/scanner; check whether the same host also dropped update.log or a known-hash artifact. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block the IPs and qaqkongtiao.com at the perimeter/EDR, and capture memory before reboot to recover the SOCKS-proxy/keylog module. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for these IOCs over 90 days, pivot on the initiating-process hash, and review for data-staging of browser/Skype credentials (UC5).

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2IPs) or RemoteUrl has "qaqkongtiao.com"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

  (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Src = "NetworkSession"),
  (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "qaqkongtiao.com" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, Src = "DNS"),

Golden Gh0st RAT credential collection from 360/QQ browsers and Skype AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Golden Gh0st RAT's data-collection stage: a non-browser process touching credential/profile stores of the specific applications the malware targets — 360 Secure Browser, 360 Speed Browser, Tencent QQ Browser, and Skype. Presence of these Chinese-market browser artifacts being accessed by a foreign process on a Western endpoint is highly anomalous. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit list of Golden Gh0st RAT collection targets (Skype, 360 Secure Browser, 360 Speed Browser, Tencent QQ Browser) plus their known credential-store filenames; scoping to a non-browser accessor keeps it high-fidelity and the Chinese-market browser paths make it distinctive for Western SOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/EDR agent enumerating user profile directories including installed 360/QQ browsers
  • Endpoint DLP tooling scanning browser credential files
  • Legitimate password-manager import utility reading Login Data
  • Browser-sync helper processes with a slightly different image name than the main browser
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MpCmdRun.exe","backup.exe","CrashPlanService.exe","code42.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the accessing process and its hash/path; confirm it is not a sanctioned backup/DLP agent and whether the credential DB was copied to a staging/Temp path. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the accessor, and force password/session resets for any credentials stored in the touched browsers/Skype. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate to update.log side-load (UC2) and C2 egress (UC4) on the same host, and check for archive creation (.rar/.zip) staging the harvested DBs prior to exfil.

author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

logsource:
  category: file_access

detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\360se6\'
      - '\360Chrome\'
      - '\QQBrowser\'
      - '\Tencent\QQBrowser\'

| TargetFileName=/\\(Login Data|Web Data|Cookies|key4\.db|logins\.json|cookies\.sqlite)$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(360se|360chrome|QQBrowser|chrome|firefox|Skype)\.exe$/i

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'

            - 'downloadstring'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

Ernst & Young is notifying customers of a data breach caused by the compromise of a third-party support ticket system used by its IT personnel. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Inside the Search for "Clean" Residential Proxies for Carding

BleepingComputer
2026-07-17 3 use cases 0 techniques 1 kill-chain phase detected

Residential proxies are no longer the silver bullet they once were for carding. Flare explains why cybercriminals increasingly seek "clean" residential proxies and combine them with browser fingerprints, device profiles, and other identity signals to evade modern fraud detection. [...]

Domainsnetnut.com netnut.io alarum.io ascarding.net

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Corporate endpoint browsing the ascarding.net carding forum · [LLM] Internal host connecting to NetNut / Alarum residential-proxy infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Corporate endpoint browsing the ascarding.net carding forum AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts resolving or connecting to ascarding.net ("The Carding Forum Asylum"), the forum hosting the 'Getting the Cleanest Possible IPs for Carding' guide central to this Flare report. Near-zero legitimate business reason for a corporate device to reach a carding marketplace, making it a high-fidelity insider-fraud / compromised-host signal. Rationale: Uses the exact carding-forum domain ascarding.net named/screenshotted in the article and confirmed via search as 'The Carding Forum Asylum' hosting the cited carding guide; corporate endpoints have virtually no legitimate reason to reach it, so it is high-fidelity with minimal enumeration. Cross-checked against: • https://ascarding.net/threads/3970/ • https://ascarding.net/forums/44/
ATT&CKT1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intelligence analyst manually browsing the forum from a sanctioned research workstation
  • SOC analyst validating an IOC during triage
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM following a URL from a feed
  • Security-vendor crawler running on corporate egress
  • User clicking an ascarding.net link embedded in a phishing/threat-report email
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("ti-research-vm01","soc-sandbox01") or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-tithreatintel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device, user and initiating process (browser vs. non-browser/automation). Confirm the host is not a sanctioned TI/research asset and the account is not a security analyst. 2) Contain: if the device is a standard corporate endpoint, isolate it, force credential reset for the user, and block ascarding.net at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for connections to netnut.com/netnut.io/alarum.io and other proxy vendors, antidetect-browser installs (e.g. Dolphin, GoLogin, Multilogin), and any access to internal payment/finance systems in the surrounding window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "ascarding.net"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "ascarding.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Endpoint DNS/Web Access to ascarding.net Carding Forum
id: 6f3b9a12-4c2e-4d7a-9f11-2a7c8e6b1d04
description: Detects a host resolving or connecting to ascarding.net, a known carding forum central to the Flare residential-proxy carding report.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/inside-the-search-for-clean-residential-proxies-for-carding/
  - https://ascarding.net/threads/3970/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|contains: 'ascarding.net'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*ascarding.net* OR *ASCARDING.NET*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/ascarding\.net/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_host="*ascarding.net*" OR All_Traffic.url="*ascarding.net*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_host="*ascarding.net*" OR All_Traffic.url="*ascarding.net*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Internal host connecting to NetNut / Alarum residential-proxy infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts corporate devices resolving or connecting to netnut.com, netnut.io or alarum.io — the residential-proxy vendor (Alarum Technologies / NetNut) whose exit nodes the FBI seized in July 2026 and which carders in this report seek for 'clean' finance-compatible IPs. A device reaching these gateways typically indicates residential-proxy client software running locally to anonymize/geo-shift outbound sessions. Rationale: Uses the four concrete vendor domains named in the article (netnut.com, netnut.io, alarum.io) corroborated by the FBI/Google NetNut-Popa seizure; DNS to these gateways from an endpoint is a strong indicator of residential-proxy client tooling rather than incidental browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/07/fbi-seizes-netnut-proxy-platform-popa-botnet/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fbi-google-take-down-netnut-proxy/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/netnut-proxy-network-disrupted-2-million-infected-devices-cut-off/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing / ad-verification team legitimately licensing NetNut for localized ad checks
  • Brand-protection or SEO tooling using residential proxies for geo testing
  • QA/localization team validating region-specific site rendering
  • Threat-intel analyst visiting the vendor site post-seizure to review the takedown
  • Security researcher enumerating proxy vendors from a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "mktg-" or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-adverify","svc-brandprotect"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine which process reached the domain (a browser tab to the marketing site is far lower risk than a headless/service binary hitting a gateway API). Check whether the user/device belongs to a sanctioned marketing or research function. 2) Contain: for non-sanctioned hosts, isolate the endpoint, hunt for and remove residential-proxy client binaries, and block netnut.com/netnut.io/alarum.io at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/user with ascarding.net access, antidetect-browser artefacts, and abnormal logins to internal finance/payment portals or customer PII stores in the surrounding window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io","alarum.io")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io","alarum.io")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by FirstSeen desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Coding Tests Deliver OtterCookie-Aligned Malware Hidden in SVG Flag Images
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 AICommand & Control High
Hunts a node.exe/npm process resolving or connecting to the REF9403 command-and-control infrastructure (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) used by the OtterCookie-aligned four-stage payload. Node is not a browser, so an interpreter reaching this dev-TLD domain family is a high-fidelity C2 signal specific to the fake-coding-test lure. Rationale: Anchors on the four confirmed C2 subdomains (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) plus a node/npm initiator so it fires on interpreter-driven C2 even though the domain is single-sourced to Elastic; a JS runtime resolving a dev-TLD attacker domain is near-zero in benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/11/contagious-interview-malware-delivered-through-fake-developer-job-interviews/ • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using a package or SaaS hosted on a *.rightwidth.dev subdomain (validate the specific FQDN against the IOC list)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned analysis VM
  • Corporate proxy/DNS-sinkhole re-resolving the domain for blocking (resolver IP, not endpoint)
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tooling actively resolving IOCs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl == "rightwidth.dev" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("threatintel","ioc-check","sandbox"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving process is node/npm and pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine to find the trojanized repo path; check whether the host cloned a repo referencing Next.js v14/NestJS/Auth.js lure stack. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block *.rightwidth.dev at DNS/proxy, and kill the node process tree; preserve the repo and node_modules for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same aid/DeviceName for reads of .claude/.cursor/.windsurf dirs, browser Login Data, and crypto-wallet extension storage, and rotate any credentials/AI-service tokens present on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "rightwidth.dev" or RemoteUrl in~ ("ldb.rightwidth.dev","upload.rightwidth.dev","controller.rightwidth.dev","rightwidth.dev")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","yarn.cmd","electron.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery endswith "rightwidth.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a Node.js process enumerating the AI coding-tool configuration directories (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .windsurf, .pearai, .llama) that OtterCookie's file-stealer module explicitly harvests for API keys, tokens and LLM conversation logs. This directory set touched by a JS interpreter is the novel differentiator in the REF9403 campaign. Rationale: Uses the exact six AI-tool config dir names OtterCookie enumerates (corroborated by Talos and cyberandramen.net) with a node.exe initiator; a JS runtime crawling .claude/.cursor/.windsurf together is behaviour no legitimate build tool exhibits. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The AI tools themselves updating their config (initiating process is cursor.exe/claude.exe, not node.exe)
  • A developer's own dotfile-sync or backup script running under node reading these dirs
  • VS Code extensions built on Node performing legitimate config reads of a single tool
  • Security tooling inventorying installed AI extensions
Suppression filter
| where DirsTouched >= 2 and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dotfiles-sync"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — legitimate access reads one tool dir; OtterCookie sweeps all six plus .env/.pem/.key/.ssh. Confirm the parent is an npm-launched project, not the AI IDE. 2) Contain: isolate host, suspend the node process, and immediately rotate all AI-service API tokens (Claude/Cursor/Gemini) and any secrets found in the swept directories. 3) Hunt: correlate with rightwidth.dev C2 (UC1) and serverValidation.js execution (UC3) on the same host, and check for browser Login Data / crypto-wallet extension reads.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount=dcount(FileName), DirsTouched=make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| summarize FileCount=dcount(TargetFilePath), Dirs=make_set(TargetFilePath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Node.js Process Accessing AI Coding-Assistant Config Directories (OtterCookie)

description: Detects a Node.js interpreter reading the AI coding-tool config directories OtterCookie's file-stealer module targets for tokens and LLM logs
references:

#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/ ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm)\.exe$/i | TargetFileName=/\\\.(claude|cursor|gemini|windsurf|pearai|llama)\\/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_paths dc(Filesystem.file_name) as distinct_files min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.claude\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.cursor\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.gemini\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.windsurf\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.pearai\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.llama\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner process_guid [| tstats summariesonly=false values(Processes.process_name) as process_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") by Processes.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`] | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | sort - lastTime
serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the OtterCookie loader serverValidation.js, which reassembles the base64 payload fragments hidden in HTML comments across the country-flag SVG images (AE.svg, AF.svg) in the repo's assets directory. Detection targets the named loader script running under node as part of the fake coding-assessment repo. Rationale: Uses the exact loader filename serverValidation.js named by Elastic plus a node interpreter; dual proc+filewrite Defender coverage catches both cmdline-visible and require()-loaded execution, so the detection survives whether the script is passed as an arg or imported. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/north-korea-linked-hackers-hide.html • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027.003 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project genuinely shipping an unrelated file named serverValidation.js (verify repo origin and whether it reads SVG assets)
  • Developer authoring server-side validation logic in a file coincidentally named the same
  • CI/CD pipeline running a benign validation step under node
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the parent repo dir, inspect the assets/ folder for country-flag SVGs (AE.svg, AF.svg) containing base64 in HTML comments, and read serverValidation.js for base64 reassembly/eval logic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node tree, quarantine the repo, and block rightwidth.dev. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same repo/loader across other developer endpoints (Slack-lure victims), and pivot to UC1 C2 beacons and UC2 AI-config-dir reads; rotate credentials on any confirmed host.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and ProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="proc", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="filewrite", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
